body:
Every sparse autoencoder trained on a language model encodes the same unexamined commitment: a feature is a ray. Latent $i$ contributes $z_i(x),d_i$ to the reconstruction, one scalar times one fixed unit vector $d_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$, and the interpretability that follows — the dashboard, the max-activating examples, the steering vector — is interpretation of that ray. Nobody argued for this. It arrived from sparse dictionary learning, where the atoms genuinely are directions, and it has been carried unmodified into a setting where there is no particular reason to think the underlying objects are one-dimensional.

Two papers posted within a week of each other in June 2026 attack that commitment from opposite ends. One proves it causes the pathology the field has been patching for two years; the other shows, empirically and at scale, that what survives a change of random seed is not the directions but the subspaces they span. Read together they say something sharper than either says alone: the sparse autoencoder has been fitting a basis for an object whose basis is not identified, and then asking us to interpret the basis vectors.

## Two years of patches on the wrong layer

The pathology has a name. Chanin and colleagues introduced [feature absorption](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.14507) in late 2024: an SAE latent that appears to track a clean concept — *starts with E* — silently fails to fire on particular instances, *elephant* among them, because a more specific latent has swallowed the general direction into itself. They pinned it down on a first-letter identification task across more than 200 Gemma Scope SAEs, a task chosen because it has ground truth, so precision and recall of a latent against a known concept are actually measurable rather than vibes about a dashboard.

Absorption is not a training failure. It is the optimum. Take a parent concept $B$ and a child $A \subset B$, with true directions $d_B$ and $d_A$, so that an $A$-token's activation contains $d_A + d_B$. An honest dictionary spends $L_0 = 2$ on every $A$-token. Now let the dictionary instead hold $d_{B \setminus A}$, firing on $B$-but-not-$A$, and an absorbed atom $d_A + d_B$ firing on $A$. Reconstruction is unchanged and $L_0$ drops to 1 on $A$-tokens. Any objective of the form reconstruction-plus-sparsity-penalty prefers the second dictionary strictly. The concept-tracking latent is punished for being a concept-tracking latent.

The remedies all accepted the ray. [Matryoshka SAEs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.17547) train nested prefix dictionaries so that early latents must reconstruct alone and therefore cannot rely on children to carry the parent. [OrtSAE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.22033) penalizes pairwise decoder cosine similarity, reporting a 65% reduction in absorption and 15% in composition while recovering 9% more distinct features. Both work, partially. Neither touches the assumption, and Chanin and Dulka later showed the assumption bites from the other side too: [feature hedging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11756), where an SAE narrower than the true feature count blends correlated features into single latents through the reconstruction term rather than the sparsity term. Width is not a neutral knob. You get hedging below the true count and absorption above it, driven by different halves of the same loss.

## Why one direction is not enough

Engels and colleagues had already shown the ray is empirically wrong. [Not All Language Model Features Are Linear](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14860) gives a criterion for a multi-dimensional feature to be *irreducible* — not decomposable into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional parts — and exhibits days of the week and months of the year as circles in activation space, with causal evidence that the circle, not any point on it, is the unit the model computes with for modular arithmetic.

Ask what a top-$k$ SAE must do with such an object, in the hardest case $k=1$. Let the feature live on a 2-plane, activation $x = r,u(\theta)$ with $u(\theta) = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)^\top$ in that plane, $r > 0$. With a 1-sparse nonnegative code and unit-norm atoms $d_j = u(\phi_j)$, the best reconstruction picks the nearest atom and sets $z = r\cos(\theta - \phi_j)$, leaving residual norm $r,|\sin(\theta - \phi_j)|$. Relative error is therefore $|\sin(\theta-\phi_j)|$, and with $m$ atoms placed to minimize the worst case they are equally spaced, nearest atom within $\pi/m$:

$$\varepsilon_{\max} = \sin(\pi/m) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad m ;\ge; \frac{\pi}{\arcsin \varepsilon} ;\approx; \frac{\pi}{\varepsilon}.$$

Hold the day-of-week circle to 5% relative reconstruction error and you need 63 latents. Not 63 latents for the concept *weekday* — 63 fragments of one circle, each of which will get a dashboard, a top-activating-examples list, and an automated explanation reading something like "Tuesday-ish contexts." In $k$ dimensions the count is the covering number of $S^{k-1}$ at angular resolution $\arcsin\varepsilon$, growing as $\varepsilon^{-(k-1)}$: exponential in the feature's intrinsic dimension. This is my derivation, not a result quoted from a paper, but it is the mechanism the June 2026 [Subspace-Aware Sparse Autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06333) paper formalizes when it argues that assigning each latent a single decoder direction *provably induces* feature splitting, and gives a criterion for when one multi-dimensional feature has been fragmented across many learned vectors.

There is a second, subtler penalty. The $\ell_1$ cost of representing $r,u(\theta)$ in a 2-atom orthogonal basis is $\lambda r(|\cos\theta| + |\sin\theta|)$, which ranges over $[\lambda r, \sqrt{2}\lambda r,\]$ as $\theta$ turns. The sparsity penalty on a rotationally symmetric feature is not rotationally symmetric. It is cheapest exactly on the axes, so the optimizer is paid to nail atoms onto whichever angles the data visits most, and the learned basis becomes a function of the empirical angular histogram. That is a recipe for seed dependence, and it is what the seed-dependence study found.

## Groups, and the gauge that makes them work

SASA's move is to replace the scalar-times-direction term with a subspace. Write the decoder as $G$ blocks, $D_g \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k_g}$ with orthonormal columns and code $c_g \in \mathbb{R}^{k_g}$:

$$\hat x ;=; b + \sum_{g=1}^{G} D_g c_g, \qquad \Omega(c) ;=; \lambda \sum_{g=1}^{G} \sqrt{k_g},\lVert c_g \rVert_2 .$$

Sparsity is now at the group level — the group-lasso norm, $\ell_1$ across blocks and $\ell_2$ within — and SASA adds a rank-adaptive regularizer so $k_g$ is learned rather than fixed. The circle now costs $\lambda\sqrt{2},r$ for every $\theta$. The angular ripple is gone, the covering-number blowup is gone, and using a feature costs something while orienting inside it costs nothing.

The consequence I find most interesting is one neither paper states in these terms, so mark it as my synthesis. The group penalty has an exact gauge symmetry: for any orthogonal $Q \in O(k_g)$, the substitution $D_g \mapsto D_g Q^\top,; c_g \mapsto Q c_g$ leaves both the reconstruction and $\lVert c_g\rVert_2$ untouched. The objective identifies $\operatorname{col}(D_g)$ and is formally indifferent to the basis within it. Standard SAEs have the same indifference *approximately* — an irreducible $k$-dimensional feature has no canonical basis either — but with a penalty that breaks the symmetry weakly and arbitrarily, so the optimizer resolves it by some accident of initialization and data order.

Which is precisely what [Unstable Features, Reproducible Subspaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.12138) measures. Training many SAEs across seeds, the authors estimate per-latent the probability that a similar latent reappears in an independently trained run, and split the dictionary into stable and unstable. Stable latents carry most of the reconstruction- and prediction-relevant signal; unstable ones have weak marginal impact and are dominated by low-frequency surface-form triggers in both their activation statistics and their automated explanations. The finding that matters here is the geometric one: the unstable latents, individually non-reproducible, *concentrate in reproducible lower-rank subspaces*. Their conclusion is that seed dependence often reflects basis ambiguity rather than noise. That is the gauge symmetry, observed in the wild, on dictionaries that were never given a group structure to be ambiguous within.

## A diagnostic you can run this afternoon

You do not need to retrain anything to check whether your dictionary is fragmenting. Take a latent you care about, collect the latents that co-fire with it, stack their decoder directions, and look at the spectrum.

```python
import numpy as np
def split_score(W_dec, idx, thresh=0.90):
    """W_dec: (n_latents, d). idx: indices of a co-firing cluster."""
    D = W_dec[idx]                       # (m, d), rows unit-norm
    s = np.linalg.svd(D, compute_uv=False)
    energy = np.cumsum(s**2) / np.sum(s**2)
    r_eff = int(np.searchsorted(energy, thresh) + 1)
    return len(idx), r_eff, len(idx) / r_eff   # (m, effective rank, split factor)
If $m$ latents co-fire and their decoder matrix has effective rank $r_{\text{eff}} \ll m$, you are looking at one $r_{\text{eff}}$-dimensional feature shattered into $m$ pieces, and the split factor $m / r_{\text{eff}}$ is roughly how much of your dictionary that one object is consuming. A cluster of 40 latents spanning a rank-3 subspace is not 40 concepts. Interpreting them separately produces 40 plausible explanations of the same thing, which is worse than producing none, because plausibility is the only check most of this literature applies.
The seed version is the same idea across runs. Do not match latents by decoder cosine — that comparison is the one the gauge symmetry breaks. Match subspaces: for candidate blocks $U, V$ with orthonormal columns, compute the singular values of $U^\top V$, which are the cosines of the principal angles, and report the mean or the Grassmann distance $\big(\sum_i \theta_i^2\big)^{1/2}$. Two dictionaries can disagree completely at the latent level and agree to within a fraction of a degree on span. Cosine-matching will tell you your SAE is unstable; principal angles will tell you which part of it actually is.
```

## What is still badly unresolved

The honest position is that we do not currently have instruments good enough to certify that any of this helps. Chanin's [audit of SAEBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18229) puts the standard metrics through reseed noise on a fixed SAE, ground-truth correlation on synthetic SAEs, and discriminability across training trajectories, and concludes that Targeted Probe Perturbation and Spurious Correlation Removal fail multiple lenses at their canonical settings and should not be used; the remaining metrics carry more reseed noise and less discriminability than the field assumes; and the most reliable one, the sae-probes variant of $k$-sparse probing, still struggles to separate variants of the same architecture. That is exactly the resolution you need to adjudicate SASA against BatchTopK against Matryoshka. Papers reporting single-digit-percent improvements on these metrics are reporting numbers within the noise floor of the metric.

Worse, [Sanity Checks for Sparse Autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.14111) freezes decoder weights at random initialization, freezes encoder weights at random initialization, and finds these baselines remain competitive with a fully trained BatchTopK SAE at $L_0=160$ across four evaluation metrics, while trained SAEs fail to recover ground-truth features on synthetic data where the answer is known. Reconstruction fidelity and feature recovery have come apart. Any claim that a new objective recovers better features has to clear a random dictionary first, and most published comparisons never ran that control.

There may also be no fix available at any price. The [rate-distortion-polysemanticity tradeoff](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14694) argues, under toy-model assumptions, that constraining an SAE to be monosemantic *necessarily* increases both rate and distortion — the three desiderata of faithful, short, and interpretable are in genuine tension, and current evaluation measures only the first two. If that generalizes, group sparsity does not escape the tradeoff; it relocates along it, buying monosemanticity with reconstruction error and paying for the appearance of an improvement with a metric that does not price interpretability at all.

And subspaces are a strictly weaker claim than directions, which should make us more careful, not less. A rank-$k$ block has $k$ times the parameters and $k$ times the license to fit whatever is there; "this 5-dimensional subspace encodes deception" is much harder to falsify than "this direction does." The gauge symmetry that makes group sparsity well-behaved is the same symmetry that makes the object less interpretable: there is no canonical vector to read off, so the steering intervention that used to be a scalar multiple of $d_i$ becomes a choice of point in a $k$-sphere, with no principle for choosing. Reproducibility across seeds is not evidence of reality either — two seeds share architecture, data, and objective, so a shared inductive bias reproduces perfectly while corresponding to nothing in the model.

I still think the direction of travel is right, and it is where the field's own [position paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23845) points when it argues SAEs should be used to discover unknown concepts rather than to act on known ones — after [Kantamneni and colleagues](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.16681) found SAE probes failing to beat logistic regression across 113 binary classification datasets, including under data scarcity, class imbalance, and label noise. Discovery is exactly the regime where fragmenting one circle into 63 latents is most expensive, because the fragments look like discoveries. If the atom is a subspace, then the last two years of dictionaries were enumerating coordinate charts and calling them concepts.

## Further reading

*A note on retrieval: arXiv, OpenReview, Semantic Scholar, the Alignment Forum and Transformer Circuits were all blocked by this session's egress policy, so the sources below were located and read through search results rather than by fetching full texts. Titles, venues, arXiv identifiers and URLs are as retrieved; reported figures are as stated in retrieved abstracts and summaries. The covering-number derivation, the $\ell_1$ anisotropy argument, the gauge-symmetry reading, and the split-score diagnostic are mine and are marked as such above.*

- *A is for Absorption: Studying Feature Splitting and Absorption in Sparse Autoencoders*, Chanin et al., arXiv:2409.14507, NeurIPS 2025. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.14507) — the paper that named the problem, and still the best example of why ground-truth tasks beat dashboard inspection.
- *Not All Language Model Features Are Linear*, Engels, Michaud, Liao, Gurnee, Tegmark, arXiv:2405.14860. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14860) — irreducible multi-dimensional features with causal evidence; the empirical premise everything above rests on.
- *Subspace-Aware Sparse Autoencoders for Effective Mechanistic Interpretability*, arXiv:2606.06333, June 2026. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06333) — decoder subspaces plus group sparsity and a rank-adaptive regularizer; the formal statement that one-dimensional latents provably split.
- *Unstable Features, Reproducible Subspaces: Understanding Seed Dependence in Sparse Autoencoders*, arXiv:2606.12138, June 2026. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.12138) — read alongside the above; basis ambiguity rather than noise, measured across seeds at scale.
- *Feature Hedging: Correlated Features Break Narrow Sparse Autoencoders*, Chanin and Dulka, arXiv:2505.11756. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.11756) — the failure mode on the other side of the width knob, driven by reconstruction rather than sparsity.
- *Learning Multi-Level Features with Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders*, arXiv:2503.17547. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.17547) — nested prefix dictionaries; the strongest fix that keeps the one-direction assumption.
- *OrtSAE: Orthogonal Sparse Autoencoders Uncover Atomic Features*, arXiv:2509.22033. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.22033) — 65% absorption reduction from a pairwise-cosine penalty that scales linearly in dictionary size.
- *Are Sparse Autoencoder Benchmarks Reliable?*, Chanin, arXiv:2605.18229, May 2026. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18229) — the audit that should change what you are willing to believe from an SAEBench table.
- *Sanity Checks for Sparse Autoencoders: Do SAEs Beat Random Baselines?*, arXiv:2602.14111. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.14111) — frozen random encoders and decoders staying competitive; run this control before believing your own results.
- *The Rate-Distortion-Polysemanticity Tradeoff in SAEs*, Mencattini, Montagna et al., arXiv:2605.14694, May 2026. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14694) — monosemanticity as a priced good rather than a free lunch.
- *Are Sparse Autoencoders Useful? A Case Study in Sparse Probing*, Kantamneni et al., arXiv:2502.16681, ICML 2025. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.16681) — 113 datasets, four hard regimes, and logistic regression winning.
- *Position: Use Sparse Autoencoders to Discover Unknown Concepts, Not to Act on Known Concepts*, arXiv:2506.23845. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23845) — the most defensible reply to the probing results, and it sharpens rather than dodges them.
